entries.title: Oktoberfest 2026: Everything you need to know
entries.summary: This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!
entries.content:
September 19, 2026

This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!

On Saturday, September 19, at noon, Oktoberfest will once again open with the ceremonial tapping of the keg, during which the mayor of Munich drives a tap into the first wooden barrel of beer and calls out "O'zapft is," a Bavarian phrase that translates to "It's tapped."

His call will be followed by 12 gunshots, a signal that lets all festival tents know that they can start serving beer.

More than 6 million people are expected at the world's largest Volksfest, which runs this year through October 4.

Expanded security measures to prevent overcrowding

The festival grounds are enormous: Oktoberfest takes place on Munich's Theresienwiese, a 34.5-hectare site roughly the size of 48 soccer fields.

But crowds can swell, especially on weekends — sometimes to dangerous levels.

Last year, officials had to temporarily close the entrances.

One reason is that nearly all 38 beer tents operate in two or three reservation shifts. When one group of guests leaves and the next arrives at the 14 large tents — which each accommodate several thousand people — huge numbers of visitors end up trying to enter and exit at the same time.

That's how, on one Saturday afternoon at last year's Oktoberfest, the crowds became so dense that movement temporarily came to a standstill. The crush caused some visitors to panic.

To prevent that from happening again, the city of Munich has overhauled its security plan for this year's festival.

Twenty-six new cameras, in addition to 56 police cameras, will monitor the grounds, while an AI system will analyze visitor flows and issue alerts if areas become overcrowded.

A newly established coordination center is also intended to improve communication between security agencies and event organizers.

Organizers and police have drawn up a plan to defend against drones over the grounds, though no details have been disclosed.

In addition, 600 police officers will be deployed on site.

Oktoberfest is famous worldwide, but most visitors are local

Oktoberfest may be known around the world as an international tourist attraction, but most of its visitors don't travel very far to get there.

A study commissioned by the city of Munich last year found that the festival remains overwhelmingly regional.

In 2025, 41% of visitors came from Munich, another 25% from the surrounding area and 9% from elsewhere in the region. In all, three-quarters of Oktoberfest's roughly 6.5 million visitors came from Bavaria. Another 4% came from elsewhere in Germany.

About 21% of visitors — roughly 1.35 million people — traveled from abroad. Americans made up the largest group of international visitors, accounting for just under 20% of the total, or more than 270,000 people. Italians were next, at just over 13%.

Beer prices rise again

Cannabis is banned throughout the festival grounds.

Alcohol, on the other hand, is available in whatever quantities visitors are willing — and able — to pay for. A Mass, the traditional 1-liter mug of beer served at Oktoberfest, costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17-$18.25) this year, only slightly more than last year.

A liter of table water comes in at a hefty €11, although the grounds also have several free drinking water fountains.

Visitors planning to enjoy one of Oktoberfest's many rides would be wise to stay relatively sober. Tickets cost anywhere from just under €5 to €14.

Germany's traditional fairground culture was officially added to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2026, and that tradition remains very much alive at the 191st Oktoberfest. According to organizers, about 90% of the festival's more than 130 fairground operators can trace their roots back to the 19th century.

The festival remains decidedly traditional when it comes to payment, too: Many vendors still accept cash only. Visitors caught without any can withdraw money from ATMs on the grounds.

Dirndl or lederhosen for Oktoberfest?

Then there's the question of what to wear.

Bavarians who take pride in doing things properly generally show up in local traditional dress.

The dirndl is the traditional dress worn by women and girls, which consists of close-fitting bodice with a low neckline, a blouse worn under the bodice, a wide high-waisted skirt and an apron.

Men wear lederhosen, the traditional leather shorts or knee-length breeches with suspenders.

For those who are not Bavarian, lederhosen and dirndls are certainly an option, but they're by no means required. Munich's event marketing department, Simply Munich, advises first-time visitors to consider renting traditional garb rather than buying it.

Be aware that locals find cheap imitations of traditional dress off-putting, as Simply Munich points out: "If you want to avoid wry looks, steer clear of Seppl hats, 'leather pants' made of cloth and garish mini plastic dirndls. With jeans and a checkered shirt, you'll definitely be more suitably dressed."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Ed Sheeran continues US tour amid Palestinian controversy
entries.summary: Pro-Palestinian protests are expected at Ed Sheeran's first gig since Macklemore was dropped from the tour. The US rapper shouted "Free Palestine" at a concert in New Jersey.
entries.content:
United States of America

Ed Sheeran continues US tour amid Palestinian controversy

September 19, 2026

Pro-Palestinian protests are expected at Ed Sheeran's first gig since Macklemore was dropped from the tour. The US rapper shouted "Free Palestine" at a concert in New Jersey.

Pro-Palestinian protesters are expected to gather in Philadelphia on Saturday at Ed Sheeran's first show since US rapper Macklemore was removed from the tour for making Pro-Palestinian comments during a performance.

Sheeran, one of the best-selling musical artists of all time, has denied responsibility for dropping the US rapper from the lineup, saying the promoter made the decision.

Why was Macklemore dropped from Sheeran's tour?

Earlier this month, while performing at the opening of Sheeran's US Loop Tour in New Jersey, Macklemore expressed pro-Palestinian sentiments.

"One of the reasons why I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine.'"

Macklemore's comments were fiercely criticized by supporters of Israel in the US and led to him being removed from the tour.

His removal sparked a backlash that saw support acts quitting and Sheeran facing a stream of criticism.

Irish folk band Beoga, Sheeran's backing act, announced it was leaving the tour. In an Instagram statement, the band said it "fully supported" Macklemore's message.

Sheeran says he is 'not complicit' in Macklemore's removal

Sheeran released a statement on Tuesday laying out his apolitical stance on the matter.

"I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine. The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy," Sheeran said.

The 35-year-old British performer said, "Upcoming tour dates had communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting."

Sheeran added that American billionaire Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium near Boston where he was due to perform, was among those demanding Macklemore be cut from the tour.

"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care," he said on Instagram on Tuesday.

"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum," the English singer-songwriter added.

Kraft said in a statement on Monday that the decision to remove Macklemore from the tour was a result of the rapper's recent comments "and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery."

Pro-Palestinian rally planned

Local groups have planned a pro-Palestinian rally near the concert venue on Saturday afternoon.

The AFP news agency cited local police as saying there would be an "appropriate police presence" to "help ensure the safety of concertgoers, employees and neighborhood residents."

Sheeran began his tour in Auckland, New Zealand, in January and is set to wrap up in Mexico City, Mexico, in December, with shows still scheduled across North and South America.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Rebels, workers, radicals: The making of 'Red Berlin'
entries.summary: Bloody May, student sit-ins and the squatter movement: Berlin has long been a hotbed for working-class organizing and radical left-wing politics.
entries.content:
September 19, 2026

Bloody May, student sit-ins and the squatter movement: Berlin has long been a hotbed for working-class organizing and radical left-wing politics.

Berlin has a reputation for being unruly. When Joseph Goebbels was appointed the Nazi Party's district leader in 1926, he described Berlin as "the reddest city in Europe besides Moscow." From the Tailors' Revolution of 1830 and the barricades of 1848, to the rise of a vast industrial working class later in the 19th century, revolution, protest and rebellion run deep throughout the city's history.

While the future German philosopher and revolutionary socialist Karl Marx was still in high school in the small town of Trier in Prussia's Rhine Province, Berlin was fast becoming a center of the country's labor movement. It was during the March Revolution of 1848, a failed attempt to create a democratic German nation-state, that the General Workers' Brotherhood was founded, one of the first workers' organizations to become active in Germany.

By the 1870s and 1880s, major industries from mechanical and railway engineering to ready-made clothing were located in the city. As the working-class population grew, this, in turn, impacted the city's political culture.

"It became more populist in a positive sense: moving away from the traditional, elitist politics of the bourgeois liberals who had long dominated Berlin, and toward the inclusion of ordinary people, since at least men were now also important voters," Axel Weipert, a historian and author of the book "Red Berlin" (2019), tells DW.

Emergence of a radical labor movement

Berlin's labor movement became increasingly radical, partly in response to heavy-handed repression under the Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. Although Bismarck created the first modern welfare state to try and undercut the rising popularity of the socialist movement, he also introduced laws banning socialist and communist organizations, newspapers and public gatherings, as well as independent trade unions.

After Bismarck resigned in 1890, the anti-socialist laws were repealed, and the ideas of Karl Marx and his fellow revolutionary socialist Friedrich Engels became the ideology of what Weipert describes as a "genuine mass movement" in Berlin. The Social Democratic Party (SPD), Germany's oldest political party, was formed out of a merger between the General German Workers' Association and the Social Democratic Workers' Party in 1875. Before World War I, the SPD was able to win far higher vote shares in Berlin than elsewhere in the country.

In 1914, the labor movement was seriously discredited when the SPD leadership and the trade unions decided not to oppose the war pushed by Kaiser Wilhelm II. But from 1916 onwards, Berlin became the center of mass labor strikes against the war. One of the earliest strikes was against the trial of anti-war socialist campaigner Karl Liebknecht. Together with Rosa Luxemburg and other left-wing radicals, Liebknecht founded the Spartacus League in Berlin, an underground group that later became the Communist Party of Germany (KPD). 

Triggered by war-weariness, severe food shortages and economic ruin, around half a million Berlin workers joined the January Strike of 1918. Supported by the Spartacus League, the anti-war strike was led by the Revolutionary Stewards, a clandestine network of factory workers and trade unions from large munitions and metal-working factories. The same group became a core organizing force behind the overthrow of the Kaiser in Berlin on November 9, 1918.

From left-wing unity to division

In the chaotic, war-torn city gripped by violent revolution, the Spartacist Uprising of 1919 was launched to overthrow Germany's provisional government and establish a republic of workers' councils. Its violent suppression, which resulted in scores of deaths — Liebknecht and Luxemburg were both murdered by soldiers of right-wing paramilitary militias — permanently fractured the political left.

As the capital of the newly founded Weimar Republic, Berlin remained a hotbed of radical politics in the interwar period. This was especially true in neighborhoods with large numbers of tenement buildings, such as Wedding, Kreuzberg and Neukölln, where thousands of factory workers lived in squalid conditions. Berlin's many large factories also created shared interests and laid the groundwork for collective action.

"Bloody May" in 1929 saw brutal attacks on illegal May Day demonstrations, which left over 30 people dead. The SPD police president of Berlin had issued a ban on all public demonstrations for May Day, which the KPD defied. In response, the police opened fire on protestors in the streets and also shot through windows in residential buildings, primarily in the working-class districts of Wedding and Neukölln.

During the Great Depression era, the SPD lost much of its support between 1929 and 1933, as joblessness ravaged the city. "Unemployment is critical — it meant that men were no longer attached to the SPD-led factory floor and trade union and the social bonds of these spaces and organizations," explains Pamela Swett, a historian at the University of Rhode Island. "Unmoored from the rhythm of daily life, men sought new bonds — new ways to feel self-respect and camaraderie with others." Some joined the KPD, which became known as the "Party of the Unemployed." Others joined far-right paramilitary groups such as the Nazi stormtroopers.

From student sit-ins to the housing crisis

After the Nazis took power in 1933, many of the labor movement leaders were killed or exiled. Then, in the aftermath of World War II, Berlin was divided into two separate political systems. East Berlin became the capital of the communist German Democratic Republic. Isolated from the Federal Republic of Germany, West Berlin deindustrialized, the labor movement weakened, and the SPD moved to the right.

During the Cold War, many left-leaning young men moved to West Berlin to evade military service. This intensified the student movement, the center of which was Berlin's Free University (Freie Universität). It was there, in leafy southwest Berlin, that historic sit-ins were held to protest the perceived authoritarianism of the government and the presence of former Nazi officials in positions of power. The fatal shooting of student Benno Ohnesorg by a police officer during a demonstration against the visiting Shah of Iran in 1967 radicalized a generation that led the widespread protests of 1968.

In the early 1970s, a housing shortage led parts of the student movement, as well as apprentices and young migrant families, to squat in West Berlin's empty buildings.

"You have migrant laborers and young laborers participating, so this was part of working-class rebellion against capitalist housing," says Ralf Hoffrogge, a labor movement historian at Berlin's Free University.

Today, as gentrification sweeps the city, Berlin is home to the strongest and most radical tenants' movements in Germany. In a 2021 referendum, 59% of voters in the city approved the expropriation of property from private real-estate companies. Hoffrogge was part of the campaign, and his 2025 book "Loud Berlin" ("Das laute Berlin") explores how the housing crisis has become a catalyst for a "socialist renaissance" in the city.

"It's not Berlin tenants against Berlin landlords. It's tenants against global capital. I think people have started to realize these contradictions, and this is why class-based policy concepts are becoming popular again."

Edited by: Brenda Haas

entries.title: Oktoberfest opens as crowds race for best beer tent spots
entries.summary: Thousands of visitors have streamed onto Munich's Oktoberfest grounds as the world-famous beer festival gets underway. Some spent the night outside the gates to secure coveted places in the festival tents.
entries.content:
Germany

Oktoberfest opens as crowds race for best beer tent spots

September 19, 2026

Thousands of visitors streamed onto Munich's Oktoberfest grounds as the world-famous beer festival got underway. Some spent the night outside the gates to secure coveted places in the festival tents.

Crowds rushed onto the Oktoberfest grounds in the southern German city of Munich shortly after the gates opened on Saturday.

Some visitors ran toward the beer tents to claim the best seats after waiting for several hours. Members of the first group in line said they had arrived at 7 p.m. on Friday with camping chairs, sleeping bags and emergency blankets.

Organizers briefly held back sections of the crowd at the entrance, allowing people onto the grounds in stages and preventing a more concentrated rush.

How does Oktoberfest begin?

Beer could not be served until the official opening ceremony at midday, when new Munich Mayor Dominik Krause of the environmentalist Greens tapped the first keg with the traditional cry of "O'zapft is" — Bavarian dialect for "It is tapped."

Krause, 36, had said he hoped to open the barrel with two or three hammer blows at his first Oktoberfest as mayor.

He then presented the first liter of beer to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU). It's the first time Söder has received the ceremonial drink from a Green mayor.

Cannon fire then signalled that beer may be served throughout the festival grounds.

How big is Oktoberfest?

More than 6 million people are expected to attend the 191st Oktoberfest, which runs for 16 days until October 4.

The festival, known locally as the Wiesn, features beer tents, fairground rides, traditional Bavarian food and live music.

Opening day was expected to bring blue skies and temperatures of up to 24 degrees Celsius (75 degrees Fahrenheit).

How much is a beer at Oktoberfest?

A 1-liter (1.8-pint) beer costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17–$18.27) this year.

The average price has risen by 2.38% compared with last year to €15.61.

An analysis found that the average price has almost quintupled since 1985, when a liter of beer cost about 6.25 deutschmarks — equivalent to €3.20 at the fixed conversion rate. Consumer prices have risen by about 120% over the same period.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: US court rejects Trump policy on third-country deportations
entries.summary: The Trump administration has deported more than 25,000 people to countries other than their own. Now a federal appeals court has put the brakes on the policy.
entries.content:
United States of America

US court blocks Trump policy on third-country deportations

September 19, 2026

The Trump administration has deported more than 25,000 people to countries other than their own. Now a federal appeals court has put the brakes on the policy.

A US federal appeals court has largely upheld a ruling blocking the Trump administration from rapidly deporting migrants to third countries without giving them a meaningful chance to raise safety concerns.

The three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in Boston said Friday that migrants must receive effective notice of their intended destination and an opportunity to challenge removal if they fear persecution or torture there.

What did the court say about the DHS policy?

The case challenges a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) policy allowing migrants with final deportation orders to be sent to countries other than their own, provided authorities have diplomatic assurances they will not face persecution or torture.

The court said the policy could deny protections to migrants sent to unfamiliar countries without notice.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court.

DHS General Counsel James Percival said on X that the policy remains in force because Friday's ruling has not yet taken effect.

"If you claim fear in your home country, DHS has the right to send you elsewhere," Percival wrote.

The order comes as two men deported by the US to Equatorial Guinea were arbitrarily detained, with police covering their heads with bags, beating them and holding them at gunpoint in a hotel turned into a detention center, the AP reported.

More than 25,000 deported to third countries

Since US President Donald Trump returned to office, his administration has sent more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.

Some of the third countries immigrants are being deported to are:

  • South Sudan
  • Eswatini
  • Uganda
  • Equatorial Guinea
  • Liberia
  • Central African Republic

The third-country deals have drawn criticism from human rights groups, as several participating nations have notoriously repressive governments and poor human rights records.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: India news: British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal granted bail after 9 years in detention
entries.summary: Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been granted bail after more than eight years without conviction. Meanwhile, India swapped its male flagbearer for the Asian Games opening ceremony over a missing kit. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India: British Sikh man granted bail after 9-year detention

September 19, 2026

Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been granted bail after more than eight years without conviction. Meanwhile, India swapped its male flagbearer for the Asian Games opening ceremony over a missing kit. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Scottish-Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without being convicted, has been granted bail
  • India is set to replace Asian Games opening ceremony male flagbearer over missing ceremonial ⁠kit
  • Counting underway in elections for the Delhi University Students' Union

Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Saturday, September 19:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up

India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up

A last-minute logistics problem has cost shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor his spot as India's male flagbearer at Saturday's Asian Games opening ceremony in Nagoya, Japan.

Kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat is set to step in instead, joining shooter Manu Bhaker, a two-time Paris Olympics bronze medalist, who will be India's female flagbearer.

Toor, who is chasing a third consecutive Asian Games gold in shot put, said he only learned of his selection as flagbearer a day earlier and that his kit was still back in India.

"I'm told that my kit will reach at 3 p.m. at the airport. Reaching the opening ceremony venue after collecting my kit from the airport on time will be very difficult," he told news agency PTI, adding that he had informed the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) that he would not be attending the ceremony.

The Indian Olympic Association said in a statement that Toor would be unable to serve as flagbearer "due to a technical issue."

The mix-up was one of several hiccups in the run-up to the Games, which open on Saturday with more than 17,000 athletes competing across more than 40 sports through October 4.

Organizers, working without a traditional athletes' village, have housed competitors in container-style huts, hotels and a cruise ship. There have been complaints over accommodation quality, transport delays, and a mistaken playing of North Korea's national anthem for South Korea's men's hockey team.

A tropical storm bearing down on the region threatens to cause further disruption as competition gets underway.

Skip next section Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody

Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody

The Delhi High Court granted bail to British national Jagtar Singh Johal in seven murder and terrorism-related cases, clearing the way for his conditional release after nearly nine years in Indian custody.

The court overturned a 2024 ruling that had denied him bail.

Johal, 39, a Sikh rights campaigner from Dumbarton, Scotland, was arrested in Punjab in 2017 shortly after he arrived in India for his wedding.

He was accused by India's National Investigation Agency of financing and courier work for the banned Khalistan Liberation Force in connection with a series of targeted killings in Ludhiana and Jalandhar districts between 2016 and 2017.

He was acquitted in a related case last year by a court in Moga, Punjab, while the Delhi cases had continued.

Johal has consistently denied wrongdoing and says he was tortured into signing a false confession. A United Nations working group ruled in May 2022 that his detention was arbitrary.

"Eight and a half years of arbitrary detention without a clear path to trial is not justice, it is unlawful suffering," UN human rights experts said in a statement earlier this year. "The prolonged uncertainty alone is a form of psychological torture."

Indian authorities have repeatedly rejected the torture allegations and insisted that due process was followed.

What did the court say in its ruling?

In its ruling, the court cited Johal's prolonged incarceration and the slow pace of the trial as grounds for bail, despite the strict conditions typically imposed under India's anti-terror law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.

The court noted that 123 witnesses were yet to be examined and that proceedings were "certainly not likely to conclude any time soon."

The court imposed strict bail conditions, including surrendering his passport, restrictions on communication and social media activity, and regular reporting to the Investigating Officer. The court did not rule on the merits of the underlying case, leaving prosecutors free to have his bail revoked if the conditions of his release are breached.

Johal's brother, Gurpreet Singh Johal, who has campaigned for years for his release and urged successive UK governments to take action, called the ruling "a huge relief," the BBC reported.

"I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the big news from and about India this weekend.

We lead our coverage with the news that British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without conviction, has been granted bail.

A UN panel in 2022 recognized it as a case of arbitrary detention, putting the Indian government's human rights record under the microscope.

The Asian Games kick off in Japan on Saturday, but it's not all smooth sailing for the Indian delegation's preparations.

India has announced a last-minute change of its male flagbearer for the opening ceremony after star shotputter Tajinderpal Singh Toor's ceremonial kit reportedly went missing.

Finally, counting is underway in elections for the Delhi University Student Union, this time under the shadow of the Cockroach Janata Party protests and the collapse of a building in the student hub of Satya Niketan.

For the latest on these stories and more, follow our blog.

entries.title: Russia votes for new parliament in controlled elections
entries.summary: Russia is holding its first State Duma election since invading Ukraine, with voting also imposed in occupied Ukrainian regions. President Vladimir Putin's party is expected to dominate the tightly controlled contest.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia votes for new parliament in controlled elections

Published September 18, 2026last updated September 19, 2026

Russia is holding its first State Duma election since invading Ukraine, with voting also imposed in occupied Ukrainian regions. President Vladimir Putin's party is expected to dominate the tightly controlled contest.

Russians were casting their ballots on Saturday to elect a new lower house of parliament, on the second day of a round of voting that President Vladimir Putin's party is all but guaranteed to win. 

It is Russia's first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Parties that support Putin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition is barred from taking part. 

Despite expectations of an easy win for Putin, the elections are widely being viewed as a referendum on the continuation of his military campaign — now in its fifth year.

The polls are taking place at a time when public sentiment is starting to shift against the war over rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections.

More than 110 million Russians are eligible to vote for 450 members of the lower house of the Russian Parliament, known as the State Duma.

Putin's United Russia party currently controls over two-thirds of the seats and is expected to retain its dominance, allowing it to continue the military campaign despite ebbing public support.

Voting held in occupied Ukrainian regions

For the first time in a Russian parliamentary election, Moscow is conducting voting in occupied parts of the Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson.

Russia claimed to annex the four regions in September 2022, although it does not fully control any of them. The annexations are not internationally recognized.

Russian authorities say the occupied territories have more than 3.5 million eligible voters. Balloting began there and in some Russian border areas in late August, earlier than elsewhere, with officials citing security concerns.

Footage from a polling station in occupied Donetsk showed voters casting ballots while an armed Russian soldier stood nearby.

Ukrainian officials condemned the voting as illegal and urged foreign governments and international organizations not to recognize either the election or its results.

Kyiv also warned that helping organize the vote could result in criminal prosecution.

Edited by: Natalie Muller and Karl Sexton

entries.title: Germany news: Campaigns wrap up in two state elections
entries.summary: Parties are campaigning for a last day ahead of polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpomerania and Berlin. And an association responsible for German sea ports says they are at high risk from cyberattacks and sabotage. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Campaigns wrap up in two state elections

Published September 19, 2026last updated September 19, 2026

Parties are campaigning for a last day ahead of polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpomerania and Berlin. And an association responsible for German sea ports says they are at high risk from cyberattacks and sabotage. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Elections campaigns are closing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin ahead of elections on Sunday
  • The elections are particularly in the spotlight as a gauge of the strength of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which won a recent state election by a landslide
  • A port union has warned that seaports are at significant risk of cyberattacks and sabotage
  • The famous Oktoberfest opens in the Bavarian capital, Munich
  • Annual anti-abortion marches are to take place in Berlin and Cologne, with some Catholic bishops expected to participate

Here is a roundup of the top headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of September 19-20, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Oktoberfest opens as crowds race for best beer tent spots

Oktoberfest opens as crowds race for best beer tent spots

Crowds rushed onto the Oktoberfest grounds in the southern German city of Munich shortly after the gates opened on Saturday.

Some visitors ran toward the beer tents to claim the best seats after waiting for several hours. Members of the first group in line said they had arrived at 7 p.m. on Friday with camping chairs, sleeping bags and emergency blankets.

Beer cannot be served until the official opening ceremony at midday, when new Munich Mayor Dominik Krause of the environmentalist Greens is due to tap the first keg with the traditional cry of "O'zapft is" — Bavarian dialect for "It is tapped."

Read more about the opening of Oktoberfest here.

Skip next section Germany's Carsten Breuer seeks to chair NATO Military Committee

Germany's Carsten Breuer seeks to chair NATO Military Committee

Germany's highest-ranking soldier, General Carsten Breuer, is standing as candidate for the post of chair of the NATO Military Committee at a vote to take place on Saturday in Copenhagen.

The post is currently held by Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone of Italy.

Breuer, 61, will contend against General Marie Annabelle Jennie Carignan, who is currently Chief of the Defence Staff in Canada.

Breuer himself is the current inspector general of the Bundeswehr, or German armed forces.

The winner of the vote would take over leadership of the NATO Military Committee from July 2027.

The head of the committee is seen as the most influential person in NATO alongside the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (Saceur), a position currently held by General Alexus G. Grynkewich of the US Air Force.

Skip next section High-profile Jewish representative calls for AfD ban

High-profile Jewish representative calls for AfD ban

Charlotte Knobloch, the former president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, has reiterated her call for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to be banned.

"A lot about the AfD reminds me today about the path the Nazis took to power," the 93-year-old Knobloch told the daily Augsburger Allegemeine.

She said the party "teems with Jew-haters and extremists" — something she said had already existed before, "but once, such parties disappeared from the scene very fast."

This would not be the case with the AfD, she said: "It has broad support in the population, not least with young people."

The party spouts hatred, including "hatred of Jews," she said.

"Unfortunately, no one has managed to clamp down on it so far, so it needs to be banned," she said, even if this is "perhaps difficult legally."

Knobloch called on voters in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday to "read the newspaper, listen to the radio and watch TV; then you can't help seeing that the AfD is a profoundly anti-democratic party."

She also warned that Jews in Germany were "literally under fire once more," with much reminding here of the 1920s and early 1930s.

"There is hatred of Jews from right, from left and from the Muslim milieu," she said.

Knobloch herself was recently the target of a death threat following the AfD's landslide victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago.

Skip next section Police raid home of aide to AfD top candidate in Berlin

Police raid home of aide to AfD top candidate in Berlin

Police this week searched the home of an aide to the top candidate for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) at Sunday's election in Berlin, Kristin Brinker, media reports have said.

Responding to the reports, Berlin prosecutors said the police had been investigating suspected violations of laws governing the use of explosives and weapons.

According to the prosecutors, the police found no evidence to support those suspicions in the September 15 search but did turn up other items of potential criminal interest.

Reports in the Bild and Berliner Zeitung dailies said the investigators had found Nazi relics and drugs in possession of the 48-year-old aide.

In comments to the Bild, Brinker appeared to downplay the significance of the police finds.

"I never had any indication that he was of that bent. He is simply a collector," she said.

Skip next section Growing sabotage risk at Germany's seaports — association

Growing sabotage risk at Germany's seaports — association

German ports on the North and Baltic Seas are facing growing risks to their security, a port association has said.

"The threat situation for German seaports has intensified considerably," Florian Keisinger, the managing director of the Association of German Seaport Operators (ZDS), told the Welt newspaper.

Keisinger said that as major hubs, ports were likely targets for cyberattacks, espionage and sabotage.

Norman Zurke, the managing director of the UVHH, an association representing the interests of employers at the port of Hamburg, told the paper that he felt cyberattacks were the main danger.

"However, the entire logistics sector is also already affected by sabotage," he said.

He said that protecting critical infrastructure was a state responsibility and called for more investment by the federal government in protective measures for the port.

Bundeswehr to hold Hamburg drills

From September 24 to 26, the German armed forces, or Bundeswehr, will be holding drills in Hamburg, entitled Red Storm Charlie, as they have in previous years.

Among other things, they will be cooperating with authorities at the port to rehearse responses to possible crisis situations and procedures for transporting troops and materiel to other locations via the sea.

Last year, some German navy corvettes were sabotaged at a Hamburg shipyard. State prosecutors investigated two employees over the incidents but have so far failed to find any culprits.

Skip next section Oktoberfest set to begin in Munich

Oktoberfest set to begin in Munich

The world-famous Oktoberfest will kick off in Munich on Saturday with a traditional ceremony where the city's mayor taps a first barrel of beer — the liquid focus of the event.

New Munich Mayor Dominik Krause of the Green Party will open the 191st edition on the Theresienwiese festival grounds in the center of the Bavarian city at noon (1000 GMT).

Read this DW preview for everything you need to know about Oktoberfest 2026.

Skip next section Campaigns wrap up ahead of Sunday elections

Campaigns wrap up ahead of Sunday elections

Parties vying for power in Sunday's elections in two German states are wrapping up their campaigns with several events.

In the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the leftist environmentalistGreen Party are both holding large rallies.

In Berlin, the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) will also be staging big events.

Other parties concluded their campaigns on Friday.

Many voters undecided

This comes as a large proportion of voters in both states seem unsure about who they will cast their ballot for.

According to the "Politbarometer Extra" survey by public-service broadcaster ZDF, 21% of voters in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and 23% in Berlin remained undecided as of Thursday evening.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a tight contest is expected between the AfD and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), while the Greens are polling around the 5% needed to enter the state parliament at all.

The state is currently governed by a SPD-Left coalition under Premier Manuela Schwesig of the SPD.

In Berlin, surveys show the CDU in a neck-and-neck race with The Left party, while the BSW could fall below the 5% parliamentary threshold.

Berlin's government currently consists of a coalition between the CDU and the SPD under CDU Mayor Kai Wegner.

Merz's future at stake

Results from the elections could have repercussions at federal level, with Merz's political future under debate after his CDU's drubbing at the hands of the AfD in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago.

Surveys in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have shown the CDU polling at just 6%.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen! You join our coverage of all things German as attention across the country is focused on two elections on Sunday: in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the city-state of Berlin.

The parties involved in the polls are holding a last day of campaign events, with particularly the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) under scrutiny after its major win in another eastern state, Saxony-Anhalt, two weeks ago.

But events in the far south of Germany will also be in the spotlight on Saturday as the world-famous Oktoberfest in Munich belies its name once more to get underway in September.

And two major so-called "pro-life" demonstrations will be taking place in Berlin and Cologne, with counterprotests also expected.

Read on here to find out more about happenings in Germany this weekend.

entries.title: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: SPD seeks to fend off AfD
entries.summary: For nearly three decades, the Social Democrats have governed Germany's northeastern state. If they can fend off the AfD, the result may boost the fortunes of the German government's junior coalition partner.
entries.content:
Germany

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: SPD seeks to fend off AfD

September 19, 2026

For nearly three decades, the Social Democrats have governed Germany's northeastern state. If they can fend off the AfD, the result may boost the fortunes of the German government's junior coalition partner.

Stretching along Germany's Baltic coast, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is known for the tourist draws of Rügen and Usedom, the quiet island of Hiddensee with the grave of playwright Gerhart Hauptmann, and the historic universities of Greifswald and Rostock, among the oldest in the country. The state is also shaped by its industrial heritage, including its shipyards and the vast nuclear power plant at Lubmin, built in former East Germany and closed in 1995.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is Germany's most sparsely populated federal state, with a population of just 1.57 million at the end of 2025. The unemployment rate in the structurally weak state stands at 8%, above the national average. At roughly 6%, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania also has by far the lowest share of foreign nationals of any of Germany's 16 federal states.

For many former East Germans, the state is associated with long summers spent at campsites and holiday resorts along the Baltic coast. It is also home to 16 national parks, more than any other federal state in Germany, and to the Mecklenburg Lake District, centered on Lake Müritz.

Yet this federal state was also the scene of some of the earliest violent attacks on asylum-seeker accommodations following German reunification. Images of burning housing blocks in Rostock-Lichtenhagen in August 1992 were broadcast around the world. That year, the number of asylum seekers in Germany reached a provisional peak of 440,000, fueling heated debates across the country.

In August of that year, hundreds of far-right rioters attacked a residential building in Rostock that housed around 100 people from Vietnam. The building was set on fire as some 3,000 local residents applauded the attackers. Miraculously, no one was killed, though many people were injured. It was the worst outbreak of racist violence in Germany since the Second World War.

Incumbency advantage may help Manuela Schwesig

Former Chancellor Angela Merkel had her electoral district in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. For around 28 years, the state has been governed by the Social Democratic Party (SPD) in coalition with various partners.

Most recently, it has been led by the popular state premier and former federal minister Manuela Schwesig. The 52-year-old heads a coalition with the socialist Left Party. Schwesig stands a good chance of ensuring that this remains the case after the election on September 20.

Schwesig, who for a long time trailed the far-right populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD) by a wide margin in the polls, has been campaigning on the slogan "The woman against blue" — a reference to the AfD's party color.

In a televised debate with AfD lead candidate Leif-Erik Holm just over ten days before the election, the state premier described the AfD as "the most dangerous party for our country, for the economy, for social welfare, and also for us women." Addressing Holm directly, she added: "You are talking the country down."

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is not an AfD stronghold

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is the only eastern German state where the domestic intelligence agency has not classified the AfD as "confirmed right-wing extremist."

The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is polling at a historic low, the lowest in any German state. A poor showing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania could further fuel debate over the increasingly unpopular chancellor. The environmentalist Greens are also fighting to remain in the state parliament, with support hovering around the 5% threshold for representation.

With a vote distribution like this, it is highly unlikely that a majority could be assembled to elect AfD lead candidate Leif-Erik Holm as state premier. After all, every party with a realistic chance of entering the state parliament has ruled out any cooperation with the AfD.

The party's lead candidate, Leif-Erik Holm, deliberately cultivates a down-to-earth image. At campaign events, he draws on his experience as a radio host, including with the public broadcaster NDR. A member of the Bundestag for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) since 2017, he repeatedly taps into widespread dissatisfaction with the government, the economic slowdown, and the comparatively difficult social conditions in the structurally weak and sparsely populated northeast.

Holm cannot match the popular SPD state premier, Schwesig, in head-to-head comparisons of the leading candidates. But the AfD's support in the polls, neck and neck with the SPD, underscores just how deeply divided Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania remains.

Governing the coastal state is unlikely to become any easier in the years to come.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Pakistan: Suicide bombing death toll rises to at least 31
entries.summary: More than 100 others have been injured in the militant attack on a police headquarters near the border with Afghanistan. Several militants were still clashing with Pakistan's security forces on Saturday.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan: Suicide bombing death toll rises to at least 31

September 19, 2026

More than 100 others have been injured in the militant attack on a police headquarters near the border with Afghanistan. Several militants were still clashing with Pakistan's security forces on Saturday.

The death toll from a suicide bombing in Kohat, Pakistan, near the Afghan border, has risen to at least 31 people, police said on Saturday, as fighting continued to rage. 

Militants stormed the district police headquarters complex at Kohat in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province on Friday.

An explosives-laden car caused a large explosion and severely damaged a mosque on a police compound.

"At least 31 people, including 16 police personnel, have been killed and more than 100 injured so far in the militant attack and suicide bombing," a police official told AFP on Saturday.

"Several militants are still holed up in the Special Branch section of the Kohat Police Complex. An exchange of fire with them has been ongoing since late last night. Their exact number remains unclear."

What do we know about the attack in Kohat?

Police said in a statement that the suicide attack occurred near a mosque as officers, their relatives and other civilians were worshipping inside.

The statement added that security forces engaged other militants in a subsequent gun battle after at least two other attackers tried to to enter the facility.

Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a local militant group linked to the Pakistani Taliban, Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), has claimed responsibility for the attack.

Government blames TTP amid attack in Afghan border area

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack and expressed sorrow over the casualties. He directed authorities to accelerate rescue operations.

Pakistan's Interior Ministry said that the "cowardly actions" of the attackers would not weaken "the nation's resolve."

President Asif Ali Zardari appeared to blame the Pakistani Taliban, or TTP (Tehreek-e-Taliban).

"The complete elimination of Fitna-al-Khawarij and terrorists operating with foreign backing is essential for national security," Zardari said, using another term for the TTP.

Pakistan blames Afghanistan for surge in violence

The attack comes at a time when relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan's Taliban rulers are already fraught. Islamabad accuses the TTP uses safe havens across the Afghan border to plot and train for attacks in Pakistan.

Pakistan blames the increase of attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the border province of Balochistan further south in large part on the Taliban administration in neighboring Afghanistan.

The Taliban rejects these allegations.

The accusations have sparked a bitter rift and even incidents of armed conflict between the neighboring countries.

Pakistan has carried out airstrikes it says targets militants taking refuge on Afghan soil, including this June.

Authorities in Kabul have in turn decried these attacks and reported civilian casualties.
